If an email that looked like it came from you asked payroll for every employee’s W-2, would anyone check first?

The IRS has warned about this scam for years. Criminals disguise an email to look like it comes from an executive and send it to payroll or human resources, asking for a list of all employees and their Forms W-2. The stolen information is then used to file fake tax returns for refunds. The IRS urges payroll staff to double-check any executive-level or unusual request for W-2s.

Regular security awareness training helps your team spot requests like this. It’s part of Simplicity Software’s cybersecurity services. Questions? (636) 681-4832

copy.linkedin:
Is a new phone part of your holidays this year? Before the old one is traded in, sold or given away, clear it out.

The Federal Trade Commission suggests a few steps:
1. Back up your data.
2. Take out the SIM card, if it has one.
3. Remove the phone from the trusted devices on your accounts, if you use two-step sign-in.
4. Restore its factory settings to erase what’s on it.

On the new phone, set it to lock automatically, keep it up to date, and set up your authenticator app if you use one.

One IT resolution worth making for 2027: a different password for every account.

Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites to see if they work, so a password used in several places can open more than one door. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency recommends passwords of at least 16 characters, each used for only one account, and a company-wide password manager. It creates the passwords, fills them in and stores them securely, so each person only needs to remember one strong master password.
